title: Income and Subjective Well-Being in Developed and Developing Countries: A Fixed-Effects Reassessment of the Easterlin Paradox
content: Does a richer nation become a happier one? This paper revisits the Easterlin paradox using a panel of 20 countries, ten developed and ten developing, observed over 2013–2022. National average happiness, measured by the life-evaluation score of the World Happiness Report, is related to the logarithm of GDP per capita, life expectancy, mean years of schooling, the Human Development Index (HDI), perceived corruption, gross domestic savings as a share of GDP and the unemployment rate. The model is estimated separately for each group with country fixed effects, which a Hausman test favours over random effects in both groups, and with standard errors that are robust to serial correlation. Happiness is markedly higher in developed countries (mean 7.07 against 5.25 on a 0–10 scale). Within countries, the logarithm of GDP per capita is positively and significantly associated with happiness in developing countries in the baseline model (0.62) but not in developed countries (0.18). Even the developing-country association is fragile: it is not significant with autocorrelated errors, when the HDI is dropped or when South Africa, Argentina or Brazil is excluded, and in first differences income growth is unrelated to changes in happiness in both groups. A significant association in developed countries (0.61) appears only when savings is measured in US dollars rather than as a share of GDP, which mostly reflects the size of the economy. The cross-country gradient is much steeper than the within-country one: with income alone, the between-country slope is 1.38 in developed and 0.68 in developing countries, against within-country slopes of 0.11 and 0.22. Among the other correlates, only perceived corruption in developed countries (with conventional standard errors) and the savings rate in developing countries are significant in the baseline model, and neither is robust to allowing for autocorrelated errors. The regressors account for only 10 and 22 percent of the within-country variation in happiness, they are not jointly significant in developed countries, and most of the variance of the error term lies between countries. The findings are consistent with a version of the Easterlin pattern: income is clearly related to happiness across countries, but within countries the relationship is weak, fragile and absent in growth rates.
